In reality, dogs and cats grow up very fast at first: at one year old they are already the equivalent of teenagers, and at two, young adults. After that, ageing slows down. In dogs, size matters too: large dogs age faster than small ones and are considered seniors earlier. Life stages and their needs Puppy or kitten (under one year) : the ideal time for socialisation and good habits. Very short training sessions, lots of play and rest. Young (1 to 3 years) : lots of energy and sometimes a "teenage phase". The time to strengthen recall and loose-lead walking. Adult : routine sets in. Keep activities that work their brain (sniffing games, puzzle toys) and keep an eye on their weight. Senior : around 7 for most dogs (earlier for large breeds), around 11 for cats. Adapt exercise, offer a comfortable bed and talk to your vet about how often to schedule check-ups. Stiffness, changes in appetite, thirst or behaviour, disorientation: at any age, an unusual change is worth a visit to the vet. For training at every age, see our dog guide and our cat guide . h: Before you start: the right gear and the right moment · "Sit": with a lure, in a few sessions · "Down": from the sit · "Stay": the "3 Ds", one at a time · If they move: it's not a failure · Using it in real life · What about a puppy?
x: Home › Tips › Sit, down, stay Teaching your dog "sit", "down" and "stay" 🐕 Dog & puppy · Beginner level · 7 min read · Updated October 26, 2026 "Sit", "down" and "stay" are the basics of life together: waiting before crossing the road, staying calm while you open the door, being patient in front of the food bowl. Good news: these three exercises are easy to learn at any age, with treats and a few minutes a day. Here is the method, step by step, without ever forcing. Before you start: the right gear and the right moment Very small, tasty treats : pea-sized, so you can give lots without filling them up. Remember to take them out of their daily food. A treat pouch on your belt: you reward at the right moment, without digging in your pockets. A quiet place : start at home, with no distractions. Short sessions : 3 to 5 minutes, several times a day, and always stop on a success. To choose well, see our comparisons: which training treats to choose and which treat pouch to choose . 🍖 Small training treats Soft and easy to break: they swallow them fast and stay focused on the exercise. See prices "Sit": with a lure, in a few sessions We use luring : the treat guides the dog into position, without ever touching them or pushing on their back. Hold a treat in front of their nose, then slowly raise it above their head, towards the back. To follow the treat with their eyes, they lift their head… and their bottom naturally goes down. The instant they sit, say "yes!" (or click if you use a clicker ) and give the treat. After 5 to 10 successes, make the same gesture with no treat in your hand , and reward with a treat from the pouch. Add the word "sit" just before the gesture, when you're sure they'll sit. Little by little, the gesture becomes more discreet. If they back up instead of sitting: the treat is too high. Keep it very close to their nose, or practise with their back to a wall. "Down": from the sit Your dog is sitting. Place a treat against their nose and lower it slowly, straight down, between their front paws. Then move it gently forward, along the floor: they lie down to follow it. As soon as their elbows touch the floor, "yes!" and treat, given on the floor between their paws. As with the sit, remove the treat from your hand, then add the word "down". "Down" is harder for some dogs, especially on a cold or slippery floor, or if they feel a bit unsure. Practise on a mat, and at first reward even a half-down: this is shaping , rewarding each small step forward.

It's exhausting, but it's rarely just a whim. Cats are naturally active at dawn and dusk. The good news: by adjusting their day, you can often get calm nights back. Why your cat meows at night Their natural rhythm : cats are hunters, most active at dawn and dusk. A cat who slept all day has plenty of energy early in the morning. Hunger : if their last meal was long ago, they wake you to ask for food. And if meowing has already got them fed, they'll do it again. Boredom : an indoor cat alone all day often lacks play and stimulation. Attention seeking : if you respond (even to tell them off), they learn that meowing works. Heat : an unspayed female in heat meows loudly and a lot, often at night. An unneutered male may also meow if he senses a female. Age and health : in an older cat, new night-time meowing can come from vision or hearing loss, hyperthyroidism, high blood pressure or cognitive decline. See your vet. Sudden change? Don't worry: cats don't take revenge. When a cat pees outside the box, they're telling you something is wrong: with their health, their litter or their surroundings. Here's how to find the cause and help them, without ever punishing them. Emergency: if your cat keeps going to the box without managing to pee, strains, cries while peeing or has blood in their urine, call your vet the same day . In male cats especially, a urinary blockage can become life-threatening within hours. Step 1: rule out a health problem This is the first thing to check, before changing anything about the litter. Cystitis, bladder stones, an infection, diabetes, kidney problems or joint pain (which makes getting into the box hard for an older cat) can all cause peeing outside the box. A cat sometimes links the litter box with pain and then avoids it. A check-up with your vet, often with a urine test, will clarify things. Step 2: peeing or marking? "Normal" peeing : a fairly large puddle on a horizontal surface (rug, duvet, laundry, floor). The cat is avoiding the box for a specific reason. Urine marking : a small spray on a vertical surface (wall, curtain, door), with the cat standing and their raised tail quivering. It's a message linked to territory or stress. Marking is much more common in cats that aren't neutered: talk to your vet about neutering if it hasn't been done yet. Step 3: check the box and the litter Cats are very particular about their toilet. The most common causes: A box that isn't clean enough : scoop poo and urine at least once a day, and replace all the litter regularly. Not enough boxes : the usual advice is one box per cat, plus one. In a house with several floors, have one on each level. A box that's too small : it should be about one and a half times your cat's length, not counting the tail. A bad location : next to the washing machine, in a busy hallway or by their food bowl. Choose a quiet corner where they can see others coming. Litter they don't like : scented, too coarse under their paws, or changed suddenly. Many cats prefer fine, unscented litter. See our cat litter comparison . A covered box : it traps smells inside and some cats feel cornered. Try an open box next to it. 🧺 Large open litter box

The good news: a dog can learn to stay home alone calmly. The key is to understand why they bark, then move forward in small steps, without ever punishing them. Why your dog barks when you leave Dogs are social animals: being alone doesn't come naturally to them, it has to be learnt. Barking can have several causes, and the solution depends on finding the right one: Boredom or not enough exercise : the dog hasn't walked, sniffed or played enough, and is looking for something to do. Noises outside : they react to the postman, neighbours on the stairs, other dogs. This alert barking comes in waves, not continuously. Separation-related distress : they bark or howl as soon as you leave, scratch at the door, drool, have accidents or chew things near the exits, and won't touch their treat. They're genuinely unhappy; it isn't naughtiness. Never having learnt : a puppy or an adopted dog has never been taught to stay alone gradually. Step 1: observe before you act Film your departures with your phone or a camera: when do they start barking? For how long? What do they do between barks? With the right habits, it decreases noticeably within a few weeks. Why puppies bite They explore with their mouths , just as a baby touches everything with its hands. They are teething , roughly between 3 and 6 months: chewing brings relief. They play the way they did with their littermates. They are tired or over-excited : the most underestimated cause. 1. Teach it to soften its bite Between puppies, a little yelp stops the game when a bite is too hard. Do the same: as soon as teeth press down, stop moving, calmly withdraw your hand and stop all interaction for 10 to 20 seconds. Then resume the game. It learns that biting hard makes the human disappear. 2. Always offer an alternative Hands aren't toys: always offer a chew toy instead. Keep chew toys within reach at all times. As soon as your puppy targets your hands: offer a toy instead. When it chews the toy: praise. This is the principle of ignoring + rewarding the alternative . 🦷 Teething toys Vary the textures (soft rubber, rope, freezable toy) to soothe the gums. See prices 3. Respect its naps A puppy needs 16 to 20 hours of sleep a day. A puppy biting frantically at the end of the day is often an exhausted puppy. Settle it somewhere quiet in its own corner with a chew toy: it often falls asleep within minutes. 🧸 A Kong-type stuffable toy Filled with wet food and frozen, it keeps puppies busy, calms them and helps them fall asleep. See prices 4. Channel its energy Replace some hand games with sniffing games: hide kibble in a snuffle mat. Sniffing is mentally tiring and calming, much more than running. 🌾 A snuffle mat An easy way to offer a calm, sniffing-based activity every day. See prices 5. These gestures are frightening, can damage your relationship and increase the risk of real bites later. The good news: you can fix it without force, just with consistency. Why dogs pull Quite simply because it works : every time your dog pulls, it moves towards what it wants to sniff. Dogs also naturally walk faster than we do. It isn't trying to “dominate”: it has simply learnt that pulling is effective. The golden rule: tight lead = we stop Left: the lead is tight, so you stop. You wait for your dog to release the tension (it turns round, takes a step back, sits). As soon as the lead is loose again: “Yes!” and off you go. It learns that a loose lead makes you move forward . It's a direct application of the Premack principle : moving towards what interests your dog becomes its reward. Recall isn't about having a “good” or “bad” dog: it's a skill, built step by step. Why your dog doesn't come back In your dog's mind, the question is simple: what's in it for me? If the smell in the grass, the dog friend or the squirrel is more interesting than you, the smell wins. And if your dog has been told off for coming back, or if every recall means “the walk is over”, it has actually learnt not to come back. The solution: make coming back the best deal of its day , using positive reinforcement . Step 1: choose a “fresh” cue If “Come!” has already been shouted a hundred times with no result, it no longer means anything. Choose a new word (“Here!”, “Touch!”) or a whistle blast, and use it only for recall. 📣 A recall whistle It sounds the same whatever your mood, and carries much further than your voice. See prices Step 2: “charge” the cue at home In the living room, with no distractions, say your word and immediately give an outstanding reward: a piece of chicken, cheese, a treat it never gets otherwise. Repeat 10 times a day for 3 days. Your dog doesn't even need to move: it is learning that this word announces something amazing. Step 3: first real recalls at short distance When it is 2 metres away and slightly distracted, say the word. As soon as it arrives: party and reward.
